newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain says only 15 pct join public sector strike.
newsitem.headline: Spain says only 15 pct join public sector strike.

text.p: Spain's conservative government said only 15 percent of its civil servants had heeded a call to strike on Wednesday against a public-sector wage freeze.

Trade unions put the response much higher. They had called two million civil servants out for 24 hours in protest against a freeze on their 1997 salaries, which the government says is vital to meet its goal of joining a European single currency.
"From early estimates we can say that around 15 percent of civil servants called to strike have gone out," chief government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told local television.
Unions said the protest would strip hospitals, schools, postal services, courts, public television stations and airports of much their staff.
But Rodriguez said that, on average, only 40 percent of post office workers had gone on strike, while in education the figure fell to 24 percent and among airport workers to just four percent.
Buses and other transport services come under a different trade union and were largely unaffected.
"There is absolute normality. Transport, schools, hospitals and public services are all working," he said.
The government's figures, which would make the stoppage one of the least successful in recent years, were in stark contrast to those provided by the trade unions.
The giant General Workers' Union (UGT) said 89.5 percent of workers had followed the strike call in Madrid, while in Barcelona, the country's second city, the figure was around 85 percent.

The conservative Popular Party government took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule. It sparked mass protests in July when it announced it would freeze public sector salaries in 1997 to get Spain into shape for the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.

The unions, led by the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) and the UGT, say the freeze violates a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise next year in line with inflation.
The government reiterated on Wednesday it would stand firm and would not back down.
